Snow totals from CoCoRaHS for March 13-14 (Fri-Sat) were 3 to 4 inches in the Flathead, 8 inches in Polson, and 7.5 inches in Ronan. A low pressure system with a cold front pushed south through the 12th, ending the high wind threat, but bringing a heavy snow threat to the mountains and lower elevations of North-Central MT. The front then stalled, continuing periods of heavy snow through the 14th when gusty winds developed across the I-15 and MT Highway 200 corridor which led to blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Copper Camp SNOTEL measured 13 inches of new snow on the 13th. On the afternoon of the 14th, Rogers Pass was reported to have had severe driving conditions and required tire chains by the Montana Department of Transportation.

Strong winds aloft brought a round of high winds to the region beginning late on the 11th through the 12th. A low pressure system with a cold front pushed south through the 12th, ending the high wind threat, but bringing a heavy snow threat to the mountains and lower elevations of North-Central MT. The front then stalled, continuing periods of heavy snow through the 14th when gusty winds developed across the I-15 and MT Highway 200 corridor which led to blizzard conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTBZH Bozeman Pass measured a 78 mph wind gust and measured an average sustained wind of 50 mph between 11:45am to 12:45am MST. A few other weather stations also measured high wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The breakdown of an upper-level ridge brought increased wind speeds aloft. The peak winds occurred on the morning of the 17th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet station MTBCH Beacon Hill measured a 69 mph wind gust. A few weather stations also measured high wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep and broad upper level trough across the western US initially resulted in a fetch of strong southerly flow aloft across the region on the 22nd. The initial impact from this was for strong winds across a few locations in north to south oriented valleys in Southwest Montana. As the fetch of stronger southerly flow moved east, the core of the upper low moved overhead, resulting in a stretch of snow, some heavy, across terrain and northerly upslope areas. Another stronger core of winds aloft combined with departing surface low pressure to result in strong northwest winds over portions of the plains through the 23rd.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed low pressure system moved across the region, creating a deformation zone that brought winter weather conditions to the Northern Rockies. The primary synoptic driver of the precipitation was an advancing frontal boundary that moved through the area during the morning and day of Thursday April 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation began as a frontal passage that moved through around 0700MST on April 2, bringing snowfall rates of nearly two inches per hour to the Discovery Ski Area. Snow continued into April 3, resulting in storm total accumulations of ten inches at Discovery and five and a half inches northwest of Anaconda. Roadway conditions deteriorated, leading to significant travel impacts on April 3. At 0239MST, chains were required for towing units on Interstate 90 between mile markers 228 and 241. A crash resulted in a right lane closure on US Highway 12 westbound at mile marker 29.5 at 0305 MST (indirect). Additionally, spun-out semi-trucks forced a right lane closure on Interstate 90 eastbound at mile marker 232 around 0355MST (indirect). At Georgetown Lake, snowfall began around 0600MST on April 2, accompanied by wind gusts near twenty miles per hour and road temperatures dropping to thirty-two degrees, before tapering off by 0300MST on April 3. Snow eventually tapered off at Homestake Pass by 0830MST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed low pressure system moved across the region, creating a deformation zone that brought winter weather conditions to the Northern Rockies. EVENT_NARRATIVE: At Lolo Pass, snow started around 0400MST on April 2 and lasted through 0200MST on April 3, accumulating approximately seven inches. Air temperatures dropped to twenty-eight degrees, with peak snowfall intensities of two inches in three hours occurring midday on April 2. At Lost Trail Pass, rain changed to snow around 0330MST, with air and road temperatures dropping into the mid-twenties, leading to a possible road freeze-up. Winds gusted to twenty-nine miles per hour throughout the day, and snow transitioned back to light rain around 0830MST on April 3. Moose Creek observed snowfall starting around 0700MST on April 2, with snowfall rates averaging one inch per hour from 0800 MST to 1100 MST, accumulating a total of six inches before ending at 0200MST on April 3.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A record-breaking winter storm impacted western Montana as a very cold trough, originating from Siberia, transitioned southeast into the region. This system coincided with an Arctic air mass pushing west toward the Continental Divide. A powerful surface low of 981 millibars broke all-time February sea level pressure records across the Northern Rockies, including a record 985.2 mb at Missoula (previous record 985.5 mb in 1963). The negatively tilted nature of the trough resulted in prolonged heavy snowfall on the morning of the 17th, particularly across northwest Montana. By February 18th, shortwaves embedded in the cyclonic flow produced convective snow showers and squalls overrunning the Arctic boundary in place. This brought isolated flash-freeze and high impact travel to the evening commute.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snowfall impacted the US-93 and US-2 corridors. Eureka received 5 inches of snow, and a nearby location, southeast of Eureka, reported 7.5 inches of snow. A CoCoRaHS observer in Marion reported 3.8 inches. Arctic air seeped south after midnight, leading to slick roads and a flipped truck reported north of Eureka at 0855MST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between May 28 and June 4, 2026, a very slow-moving upper-level low-pressure system  over Montana tapped into moisture from the Gulf of America, bringing heavy and widespread precipitation to western Montana. Prior to this event, several locations had already received significant moisture in May, leaving soils saturated and mountain runoff elevated. The combination of intense rainfall and ongoing snowmelt led to swollen rivers, and overwhelmed small streams, and flooded local irrigation canals. Intense thunderstorms brought heavy rain-rates in Sanders County resulting in mudslides.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread small stream, agricultural, and infrastructural flooding occurred across the Mission Valley due to accelerated snowmelt and 4 to 6 inches of rainfall over a four-day period. A private weather station located 3 miles east-northeast of Pablo measured a total of 5.09 inches of rain from Friday through Monday, while another station just north of the Mission Reservoir measured 3.46 inches. Initial minor flooding began on Friday evening, May 29, when a storm dropped 0.50 to 0.60 inches of rain along the eastern side of the valley, flooding one-third of a private property near St. Ignatius. Runoff rapidly filled local irrigation systems, causing widespread issues.  |At 0600MST on May 31, the lower cylinder flood gate at Mission Dam failed during a high-flow period. While flows were already elevated, this mechanical failure induced a dynamic flow condition where discharges dropped momentarily until emergency teams opened the upper cylinder gate to stabilize the dam, returning outflow into Mission Creek to approximately 350 CFS. At 1000MST, Agency Creek breached its banks, flooding low-lying pastures between Jocko and Agency Roads. At 1300MST, North Crow Creek overflowed, inundating properties along Minesinger Trail. |At 1430MST, the Pablo Feeder Canal experienced a structural failure at Skyline Drive and Caffrey Road, flooding adjacent crop fields. A multi-agency emergency response deployed heavy equipment and placed over 500 sandbags to reinforce the canal's south wall and repair the road base. |On June 1, NWS storm surveys documented extensive field flooding along Red Horn, Hillside, and Foothills Roads due to out-of-bank tributaries. North Crow Creek completely left its banks around Timberlane Road, inundating driveways and spreading water within 1 to 2 feet of a home's foundation. Floodwaters along the Pablo Feeder Canal completely submerged a length of Minesinger Trail and Mountain View Road, rendering them impassable to traffic. At 1400MST on June 1, with the Kicking Horse Reservoir at full capacity, all active water diversions from South Crow into the reservoir ceased. This forced the unbuffered, full natural flow from the South Crow drainage directly downstream into Crow Creek. The resulting surge caused Crow Creek to leave its banks entirely, backing up directly into a commercial greenhouse business (Bev's Bloomers). The floodwaters came within one foot of an adjacent home's foundation, and left a 6-foot property fence completely underwater. Severe road washouts were also reported north of Arlee on Saddle Mountain Road, where heavy rains stripped away soil and gravel to expose bedrock. Debris, mud, and water gushed across Highway MT-35 at milepost 10 on Monday evening, carrying a boulder the size of a small car onto the driving lanes near Woods Bay.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front, combined with scattered thunderstorms embedded in southwest flow, interacted with an anomalously warm and dry air mass across southwest Montana. High temperatures were in the 80s, creating large dewpoint depressions. High winds aloft, reaching 65 knots between 16,000 and 18,000 feet MSL, were brought to the surface by both convective downdrafts and evaporative cooling, as well as the passing cold front. This synoptic setup led to severe and high wind gusts across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An initial thunderstorm produced a 54 MPH wind gust just west of Homestake Pass at 1254MST. This gust resulted in a power outage that lasted until 1930MST. Later, at 1629MST, a 67 MPH wind gust was measured at the Bert Mooney Airport (KBTM). This severe gust was associated with a weak thunderstorm that mixed down stronger winds from aloft, aided by evaporative cooling. The strong winds caused a tree branch to fall onto a car.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front, combined with scattered thunderstorms embedded in southwest flow, interacted with an anomalously warm and dry air mass across southwest Montana. High temperatures were in the 80s, creating large dewpoint depressions. High winds aloft, reaching 65 knots between 16,000 and 18,000 feet MSL, were brought to the surface by both convective downdrafts and evaporative cooling, as well as the passing cold front. This synoptic setup led to severe and high wind gusts across the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Non-convective winds occurring behind a cold front resulted in high winds across the zone. In the city of Deer Lodge (Powell County), a 53 MPH wind gust was measured at 1754MST, which blew a few shingles off a roof. The DRLM Agrimet station south of Deer Lodge measured gusts up to 49 mph between 1800MST and 1815MST. MacDonald Pass also recorded a 55 MPH wind gust. At 1815MST, a 59 mph wind gust was measured at Warm Springs (Deer Lodge County).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unseasonably cold upper-level trough, originally an Aleutian Low/Gulf of Alaska low, was dislodged and sagged south over the Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies. This system brought a prolonged period of late-season winter weather, including persistent graupel showers, accumulating mountain snow, and record or near-record cold temperatures leading to widespread frost and hard freezes across Western Montana.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The mountains generally above 5500 feet saw 3 to 7 inches of snowfall. Backcountry roads became slushy. This system also brought cold mornings with lows ranging from 24 to near freezing, producing frost. On the morning of May 17, temperatures dropped to 31 degrees at Little Bitterroot Lake, 33 degrees at Happy's Inn, 34 degrees in Yaak, and 40 degrees in Libby. By the morning of May 18, temperatures further fell to 24 degrees at Little Bitterroot Lake, 26 degrees at the Stillwater RAWS, 29 degrees in Kila, and 32 degrees at Crystal Creek.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strengthening upper level trough across CA and vicinity sent an embedded wave northeastward toward the Northern Rockies Feb 17, which resulted in surface low pressure developing and moving across Southwest Montana. This resulted in a strong cold front progressing through the area, bringing brief snow squalls, synoptic high winds, localized impactful snow, and very cold wind chills to various portions of the region into Feb 18.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow squall. ASOS station KDLN Dillon Airport measured a 53 kt gust along a cold front, which resulted in a quick transition from rain to snow at the ASOS. The visibility sensor was inoperable at the time, but the sensor did estimate moderate snow as the strong winds moved through (ASOS needs visibility to be 1/2 SM to report this). Given this estimate of 1/2 SM visibility or less, it is deemed sufficient for SQW criteria.
